extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, patent agents, and law students working on Canadian patent obviousness issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing obviousness under Canadian patent law (Windsurfing/Sanofi approaches), including how to identify the person skilled in the art, common general knowledge, inventive concept, differences from prior art, and secondary factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: The invention (identify inventive concept / claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the inventive concept of the claim in question or, if that cannot readily be done, construe it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining 'what is the invention as claimed' is a prerequisite for obviousness. For each claim in issue determine the inventive concept; where the claim is a bare chemical formula or otherwise does not reveal inventiveness, it is acceptable to read the specification to determine the inventive concept (e.g., selection patents). For New Act patents consider s.28.3 requirements when assessing obviousness of the subject-matter defined by a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: The hypothetical skilled person (the person skilled in the art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the notional 'person skilled in the art' to whom the patent is addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notional skilled worker is ordinary, lacks imagination, inventiveness or intuition, has no benefit of foresight or assurance of success, but has a sense of reasonable possibilities. The Court must place itself in the position of this technician when assessing obviousness. It would be nonsensical to ask whether an inventor or the judge today would find the invention obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: The body of knowledge of the person of ordinary skill (common general knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the relevant common general knowledge of the notional skilled person — what they may reasonably be expected to know and to be able to find out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common general knowledge includes the normal skill and knowledge workers in the field ought to know or be able to find out by routine reference to standard texts/resources; it is not a memory test. The skilled person is presumed reasonably diligent and may refer to standard texts. The state of common general knowledge at the relevant time is a question of fact and the party attacking the patent bears the burden of adducing evidence of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: The climate in the relevant field (motivation / state of the art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the climate in the relevant field at the time the alleged invention was made and the motivation in existence to solve a recognized problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the prevailing attitudes, priorities and incentives in the field at the priority date. Whether there was a motive in the prior art to find the claimed solution is relevant to whether a skilled person would be led to the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to solve a recognized problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether there was a motivation at the relevant time to solve the recognized problem addressed by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation can be found in prior art, the art itself, or common general knowledge. It can support combining references or point away from combination. Motivation is a distinct element in the multi-step obviousness inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and effort involved in the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent, nature and amount of effort required to achieve the invention (routine trials vs prolonged/arduous experimentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If achieving the invention required only routine trials, that points toward obviousness; if experimentation was prolonged and arduous, that points against obviousness. Consider whether steps would have been routine or would have required inventive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success (secondary factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success of the invention may be considered as a secondary factor in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success is a non-exhaustive secondary consideration that may prove instructive in assessing obviousness; its weight depends on evidence linking the success to the inventive features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meritorious awards (secondary factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition such as meritorious awards may be adduced as a secondary factor in the obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards can be considered as part of secondary factors that may be instructive, but their probative value depends on the quality and relevance of the evidence presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windsurfing four-step approach
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-step methodology to structure the obviousness inquiry: (1)(a) identify the person skilled in the art; (1)(b) identify their common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept of the claim or construe it; (3) identify differences between the state of the art and the inventive concept; (4) consider whether those differences would have been obvious to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court of Canada endorsed the Windsurfing approach as a useful tool but not a mandatory, rigid test. Failure to explicitly follow the structure does not by itself amount to an error of law. The approach should be applied expansively and flexibly, taking into account any secondary considerations that prove instructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanofi 'obvious to try' test (application in experimental fields)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate (e.g., pharmaceuticals), consider whether the invention was 'obvious to try' — that it was more or less self-evident to try the identified approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanofi requires evidence on a balance of probabilities that it was more or less self-evident to try to obtain the invention; mere possibility is not enough. Non-exhaustive factors (para. 69 of Sanofi) include: (1) is it more or less self-evident that what is being tried ought to work and are there a finite number of predictable solutions; (2) the extent, nature and amount of effort required (routine vs prolonged); (3) whether there is a motive in the prior art to find the solution. The 'obvious to try' test is distinct from the U.K. 'worth a try' test which tolerates mere possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mosaicing / combining prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible to combine prior art references (mosaic) to arrive at the invention, but the combination must be persuasive and motivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining references A + B = invention is allowed, but courts will ask whether the documents or the art provide motivation to combine them or point away from combining them. Limit the number of references combined: the more references required, the less obvious the path. The ease with which references would be found and their relative importance may be questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot focus on selected prior art in isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness must be assessed with regard to the whole of the relevant prior art, not a carefully-selected subset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting only a small group of publications that together point to the invention may give a misleading result; courts expect consideration of the entire field, and parties should point to other accessible prior art which might take the skilled person away from the claimed direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility of public knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on public knowledge, weight is given according to accessibility and the efforts required to find it; the notional worker is expected to have access to information available through reasonably prudent searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appropriate search is a question of fact. It is artificial to assume every obscure or archived document would be found; an obscure discarded scrap in an archive should not automatically render the invention obvious. Prior activities not publicly available are not part of the skilled person's knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper patents are viewed with scepticism (patent specifications not automatically common general knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual patent specifications do not normally form part of common general knowledge unless so well-known in the industry that they form part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For something to be common general knowledge it is not enough that it appear in a journal or be widely circulated; it must be generally regarded as a good basis for further action. Courts treat 'paper patents' (patents only on file) skeptically unless evidence shows they were accepted and acted upon in the relevant art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept may require looking to the specification (selection patents special rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claim language does not reveal inventiveness (e.g., bare formulas), it may be necessary to read the specification to determine the inventive concept, particularly for selection patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanofi accepted that the inventive concept can be found in the specification when claims are insufficient to reveal it. This can resurrect considerations akin to 'spirit of the invention' for the purpose of identifying inventive concept, but claim construction principles still delimit the monopoly; for New Act patents, s.28.3 frames obviousness with regard to prior disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewed without hindsight / avoid using court's present knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether differences between prior art and the inventive concept would have been obvious to the skilled person when viewed without any knowledge of the alleged invention (i.e., avoid hindsight reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The question is whether the steps from prior art to invention would have been obvious without hindsight. Requiring a 'degree of invention' along the way may set the test too high for inventions born of experimentation; courts must be careful not to conflate hindsight with legitimate inference from the prior art and common general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of adducing evidence of common general knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The party attacking validity bears the burden of adducing evidence about the state of common general knowledge at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because common general knowledge is a question of fact, evidence must be presented (e.g., textbooks, expert testimony) to establish what skilled workers reasonably knew or would have known and acted upon at the priority date.
